paras: The lynching of Martin Becket was the killing of a Black man taken from the jail at Hampton Courthouse, South Carolina, on the night of Tuesday, July 25, 1882. Becket had been jailed on an accusation of assaulting a white girl about twelve years old, and a crowd reported at some three hundred took him out and lynched him. A placard reading "Our women must be protected" was left with his body, and its words became the headline under which the story ran across the country.

Becket was committed to the Hampton jail on Saturday, July 22, charged with assaulting or "outraging" a young white girl whom no paper named. The Eureka Daily Sentinel identified him as "colored," and the Newberry Herald called him "a negro."

Three nights after his committal, Becket was taken from the jail by force. A dispatch from nearby Varnsville said he was lynched "by parties unknown" and that the crowd numbered some three hundred, a figure the Newberry Herald also gave. The Newberry Herald and the Watertown Republican said he was hanged; no paper said where. According to the Charleston dispatch, the placard was on his body, while the Varnsville account said it was found near the body.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry into the lynching appears in the coverage.

The news went out in a short Charleston dispatch dated July 26 that ran the next day in the Richmond Dispatch, the Washington Evening Star and the Knoxville Daily Chronicle. Western papers on July 28 printed it under a Wilmington, Delaware, dateline, and in rewriting it some placed Hampton in Delaware or North Carolina and garbled the name as Bunkett, Brickett or Breckett. Weekly news summaries carried one-line versions into early August, among them "Morton Beckett" in eastern dailies and "Martin Beckel" in a New Hampshire weekly.

Most papers adopted the mob's own words as a headline, "Our Women Must be Protected," and others headed it "A Ravisher Lynched" and "Speedy Justice." The Watertown Republican called Becket "a colored libertine," treating the accusation as proven. In South Carolina the Newberry Herald set the case among weekly reports of rapes "by some negro in this State" and wrote that "The only way to stop this crime is to keep on hanging the criminals." No paper in the coverage questioned the accusation or condemned the lynching.

The Memphis Daily Appeal put the lynching on Wednesday night, against the Tuesday night of the July 26 South Carolina dispatches and the Newberry Herald's "25th ult." The Pickens Sentinel's copy of the Charleston dispatch gave the committal as Thursday rather than Saturday, and the Varnsville account put it on the 22d, a Saturday.

reader.title: Lynching of Martin Becket
bases: A Black man held in the Hampton jail on an accusation of assaulting a white girl was taken from the jail at night by a crowd reported at some three hundred and killed (A3, A26, A24).

Becket was taken by force from jail and lynched, hanged in the Newberry Herald's account, by 'parties unknown' numbering some three hundred, who left a placard reading 'Our women must be protected' (A26, A24, A3); the killing punished an alleged assault on a white girl outside any court (A1, A26).

The Charleston wire dispatch (A3, A4) and a separate Varnsville, S.C., dispatch with added local detail (A26) agree on the jailing, seizure and lynching, and the Newberry Herald independently gives the date and crowd size (A24).

accounts.label: Charleston wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Becket, committed Saturday for outraging a white girl of twelve, was taken from jail the previous night and lynched, with a placard on his body reading 'Our women must be protected.'

accounts.label: Varnsville, S.C., dispatch
accounts.gist: Committed on the 22d; taken from jail by force by 'parties unknown,' a crowd of some three hundred; the placard was found near the body.

accounts.label: Newberry Herald (S.C.) editorial
accounts.gist: A negro named Martin Becket was taken out of jail at Hampton by three hundred men on the 25th and hanged; the paper said the way to stop the crime was to keep hanging.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Charleston wire brief verbatim, many under the placard's words 'Our Women Must be Protected' as a headline.
Western headlines 'A Ravisher Lynched' and 'Speedy Justice' and the Watertown Republican's 'a colored libertine' treated the accusation as fact.
The Newberry Herald wrote that 'The only way to stop this crime is to keep on hanging the criminals.'

conflicts.note: The Charleston and Varnsville dispatches dated July 26 say 'last night', and the Newberry Herald gives the 25th; the Memphis 'Wednesday' is a lone later rewrite.
Only the Pickens Sentinel's reprint of the Charleston dispatch says Thursday.
Western reprints carried a Wilmington, Del., dateline and some moved Hampton to Delaware; the South Carolina dispatches are the better evidence.
